topic: Gupta Empire and Harsha of Indian History
description: The Gupta period is widely regarded as the 'Golden Age' of Indian History due to unprecedented advancements in art, literature, and science. Following the decline of the Gupta Empire, Emperor Harshavardhana of the Pushyabhuti Dynasty successfully reunited and consolidated North India.

sections.title: Major Rulers of the Gupta Empire
sections.description: Chronological overview of the powerful emperors of the Gupta Dynasty and their significant political and military campaigns.

historical_events.significance: Founder of the Gupta Dynasty who assumed the title of 'Maharaja'.
Started the Gupta Era (319-320 CE) and was the first to assume the supreme title of 'Maharajadhiraja'.
Known as the 'Napoleon of India' (by historian V.A. Smith) for his extensive military conquests. His court poet Harishena composed the Allahabad Pillar Inscription (Prayag Prashasti).
Defeated the Sakas (Western Kshatrapas) and made Ujjain his second capital. The Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien visited India during his reign.

important_facts.fact: Kumaragupta I was the founder of the world-renowned Nalanda University.
Skandagupta was the last great Gupta ruler who successfully repelled the fierce invasion of the Hunas from Central Asia.

sections.title: Gupta Administration and Economy
sections.description: Key aspects of administrative divisions, land revenue systems, and the coinage of the Gupta period.

key_concepts.explanation: Provinces in the Gupta Empire were called Bhuktis, and they were governed by a provincial governor known as the 'Uparika'.
Provinces (Bhuktis) were further divided into districts called Vishayas. The head of a district was called the 'Vishayapati'.
A system of tax-free land grants given primarily to Brahmins and temples, which became highly prevalent during the Gupta period.

important_facts.fact: Gold coins issued by the Guptas were called 'Dinar', and silver coins were called 'Rupayaka'.
The primary land tax, known as 'Bhaga', generally amounted to 1/4th to 1/6th of the total agricultural produce.

sections.title: Golden Age of Literature and Science
sections.description: Prominent scholars, literary works, and groundbreaking advancements in mathematics, astronomy, and medicine during the Gupta era.

key_associations.extra_info: A world-famous Sanskrit play written by Kalidasa, who was one of the 'Navaratnas' (Nine Gems) in the court of Chandragupta II.
A seminal mathematical and astronomical text where he formulated the concept of zero and stated that the Earth rotates on its own axis.
An extensive encyclopedia covering topics ranging from astronomy and planetary movements to architecture and cloud formation.
An ancient Indian collection of interrelated animal fables designed to teach morals and statecraft (Niti-shastra).
Written by the 'Father of Surgery', this foundational medical text contains the earliest known descriptions of plastic surgery (rhinoplasty).

important_facts.fact: The major Puranas and the great Indian epics, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, were compiled into their final written forms during the Gupta period.

sections.title: Harshavardhana and the Pushyabhuti Dynasty
sections.description: The rise of Thanesar's Pushyabhuti Dynasty and the achievements of Emperor Harsha in 7th century CE.

historical_events.significance: Harsha shifted his capital from Thanesar to Kannauj and is often regarded as the last great Hindu emperor to unify North India.
Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya Dynasty decisively defeated Harsha on the banks of the Narmada, halting Harsha's expansion into South India.

key_concepts.explanation: A massive religious assembly organized by Harsha to honor the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang and to widely propagate the Mahayana sect of Buddhism.
A grand festival held every five years at Prayag (Allahabad) where Harsha famously donated all his personal wealth to the poor, ascetics, and priests.

key_associations.extra_info: Banabhatta was Harsha's court poet; the 'Harshacharita' serves as a detailed historical biography of Emperor Harsha.
These three highly acclaimed Sanskrit plays were authored by Emperor Harshavardhana himself.

sections.title: Accounts of Chinese Travelers
sections.description: Valuable historical records left by Chinese Buddhist pilgrims who visited India to collect Buddhist texts.

key_associations.extra_info: Fa-Hien visited during the reign of Chandragupta II. His accounts highlight the general peace, low taxation, and extreme prosperity of the Gupta Empire.
Visited during Harsha's reign and is known as the 'Prince of Pilgrims'. He provided extremely detailed descriptions of India's social, religious, and economic life.

important_facts.fact: Hiuen Tsang spent several years studying Mahayana Buddhism at Nalanda University, which was then headed by the renowned scholar Shilabhadra.
